newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean won rebounds on tough central bank talk.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean won rebounds on tough central bank talk.

text.p: The South Korean won rebounded from a record low on Tuesday following strong words by the central Bank of Korea (BOK), but dealers said that without swift action the local currency was doomed to fall again.
The currency closed at 870.50 to the dollar after hitting 887.00, its weakest level since a market average system was launched in March 1990.

Traders said the won recovered ground after a senior BOK official said the central bank would take "strong measures which are different from the past" to stabilise the won against the U.S. dollar. He did not specify what those measures would be.

Dollar sales by the central bank and news that the Finance and Economy Ministry was considering expanding the foreign shareholding ceiling earlier than scheduled also helped the local unit recoup losses.
South Korea had earlier said it would raise the foreign stock ownership ceiling to 23 percent some time this year from 20 percent, but a specific date has not been set.
But traders said that unless the central bank was willing to put its tough words into action, simply talking about stabilising the won would not rescue the currency.
"The central bank is trying to bluff the dollar down but no one believes they're holding any strong cards," said a Western bank dealer.
The managing director of a local bank said if the central bank was serious about stabilising the won, there were several options available.
"It could keep on intervening, it could reduce the interest on dollar deposits to make holding dollars less attractive, or, less likely, it could raise won interest rates," he said.
The central bank has refused to confirm or deny talk of its intervention in the interbank market.
The won has fallen by about 10 percent against the U.S. dollar since last June, pressured by a ballooning trade deficit and the U.S. currency's strength on world markets.
South Korea suffered a record monthly trade deficit of $3.48 billion in January, against a shortfall of $2.13 billion a year earlier.
"The market's demand for dollars is far stronger than the central bank's determination to stop its rise," said a European bank dealer.
Dealers said monthly dollar demand was currently at around $4.0-$5.0 billion.
Central bank officials blamed the won's recent plunge on bullish sentiment toward the dollar and speculative trading.
"Depreciation in the won due to economic factors is tolerable, but we will definitely block speculation and sentiment-related falls," senior central bank official Shim Hoon told Reuters.
"If we look at the abnormal rise in local foreign exchange holdings, we can see that speculation and sentiment is a major factor," he added.

As of February 10, local foreign exchange holdings had soared 133 percent to $3.5 billion from $1.5 billion at the end of 1996. This compares with a 44 percent rise to $1.13 billion from $784 million in the same period last year, according to the central bank.

While a weak currency is theoretically useful in boosting exports, South Korea has not fully benefitted because the yen is also falling rapidly against the dollar. South Korea and Japan are fierce competitors in overseas markets.
The falling won also raises the spectre of inflation. A central bank statement said that for every one percent decline in the won's value, the consumer price index rose by 0.14 percent.
Inflation rose 4.7 percent year-on-year in January, against a 5.1 percent rise a year earlier.
